name: Sam Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for seeing me, Sam. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and nothing you say will carry your name. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a shuttle car underground at a potash mine, a low flat machine that carries the ore from the cutting machine back to the conveyor belt. Day shift starts at seven, nine hundred metres down. I milked cows for thirty-one years on my father's farm until the milk price wouldn't cover the feed bill, and we sold up three years ago. So at fifty-five I was the oldest man in the induction room by twenty years.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Humbling, I'd say. On the farm I was the boss; down here I'm the one getting told off for clipping the rib, which is the side wall. My section foreman, Ray, is younger than my eldest son. But it's honest work, the pay is steady, and Irina doesn't have to worry about the bank every winter anymore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've said all along: it was mostly talk from people in cities who've never done a day's physical work. At church I'd say thank the Lord for common sense. I don't go online much, apart from the weather and the cattle prices out of habit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it'd confirm what I already believe. A machine is a tool, and somebody still has to work. I'd get my years in and retire at sixty-five with the farm money and my mine pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going exactly as I am. I'd keep learning the shuttle car so Ray stops yelling at me, and maybe get trained on the roof bolter next year. Irina and I would keep putting a bit aside each month, and I'd keep helping my son on his small beef block on weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a dry harvest week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you mean, the farm money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: After the bank took its share, there wasn't much left, about four months of living costs. We put it aside and didn't touch it. That's the cushion, along with what I save from the mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything about this picture bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only the way the companies talk. They'll use any excuse, robots or otherwise, to keep wages flat. But I'm not one for unions either, so I'd just keep my head down.

S0.say: I'd say it was mostly talk from city people who've never done a day's physical work. At church he'd thank the Lord for common sense.
S0.think: It would confirm his belief that a machine is just a tool and someone still has to work. He'd get his years in and retire at sixty-five on the farm money and his mine pension.
S0.do: Keeps going as he is, learning the shuttle car and possibly the roof bolter next year. Keeps saving with Irina each month and helps his son on his beef block at weekends.
S0.feel: Calm, like a dry harvest week.
S0.quote: A machine is a tool, and somebody still has to work.
S0.fieldNote: Sam brings a farmer's worldview underground: honest work, faith and self-reliance. He distrusts both city talk about AI and unions. Losing the family farm has made him value steady pay over anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should stand on their own two feet and learn what they need to. But I'd also say a company that's done well out of men like us owes them something. I wouldn't post about it; I'd say it after church to whoever would listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it worries me. I've heard they've already got shuttle cars at other mines that drive themselves. I'm junior and slow, and I'm no good with computers, so if they're cutting, I'm the obvious one to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut back where we can straight away: no new ute, no trip to see Irina's sister. I'd ask Ray if I could move onto the roof bolting crew, which still needs a man to handle the bolts. And I'd wait to see what the company actually does before doing anything rash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like seeing dark clouds over the hill when you've got hay down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you consider any training on the new systems?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be lying if I said yes. I sent my first email last year, and only because my granddaughter stood behind me. I'd rather learn to bolt a roof than learn to stare at a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you lost the job, would you look to the government for help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not if I could help it. I'd lean on my family first, and the church. My son's said there's always work on his block, even if it pays in beef and not much cash.

S1.say: I'd say people should stand on their own two feet, but a company that has done well out of workers owes them something. He'd say it after church rather than online.
S1.think: He worries because he's heard of self-driving shuttle cars at other mines. As a slow junior who's no good with computers, he'd be the obvious one to cut.
S1.do: Cancels the new ute and the trip to Irina's sister. Asks to move onto the roof bolting crew and waits to see what the company does before acting further.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like dark clouds over the hill with hay on the ground.
S1.quote: I'd rather learn to bolt a roof than learn to stare at a screen.
S1.fieldNote: His traditional values show in preferring family and church over government help. His resistance to technology is firm and he says so plainly. He looks for the hands-on corner of the mine, roof bolting, rather than retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what happens when big tech companies and governments in the capital push things on people without asking them. I'd vote against anyone who cheered it on. At work I'd say we'd better look after each other, because nobody else will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it frightens me. I lost a farm I thought my grandson would run. Now I'd lose this too, at fifty-nine, with a few months' savings and no other trade but cows and a shuttle car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop all spending except the essentials in the first week. I'd pray on it, and I'd talk with my son about working his block for my keep if it comes to it. I'd look at drawing the mine pension early, small as it is, and Irina would take on more hours at the bakery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Same pit in the stomach as the day we signed the farm over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Irina that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, we've weathered worse. And we have. But I'd probably sit up on the porch after she'd gone to bed, the way I did the night before the farm auction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd lean on family rather than government. Would that hold here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want it to. But if everybody's out of work at once, my son's block won't feed us all. I suppose I'd swallow my pride if it meant the grandkids eating.

S2.say: I'd say this is what happens when big tech and governments push things on people without asking. He'd vote against anyone who cheered it on and tell workmates to look after each other.
S2.think: It frightens him: after losing the farm he'd lose this job too at fifty-nine, with only a few months' savings. His only trades are cows and a shuttle car.
S2.do: Cuts to essentials in the first week and plans to work his son's block for his keep if needed. Looks at drawing his small mine pension early while Irina takes more hours at the bakery.
S2.feel: Alarmed, with the same pit in his stomach as the day they signed the farm over.
S2.quote: I'd probably sit up on the porch after she'd gone to bed, the way I did the night before the farm auction.
S2.fieldNote: The two-year picture brings back the loss of his farm, and that memory drives his alarm. He blames big tech and distant government rather than AI itself. He admitted he'd accept government help if it came to feeding his grandchildren, which goes against his principles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time for people to get ready the old-fashioned way: work hard, save and look after your own. I'd say it at church and to anyone at work who asked. I'd still say the people pushing this don't live in towns like ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be sixty-three. If the mine keeps a few older men on during the switchover, I could make it close to sixty-five. But I'm the junior, so I wouldn't bet the farm on it, if I still had one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save every spare dollar for those years, aiming to double the cushion. I'd try to get onto the roof bolters or the maintenance crew, where a pair of hands might still be needed. I'd help my son build up his beef block so there's somewhere to land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with something to do about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would building up your son's block involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More fencing, a bigger dam, maybe twenty more breeders. I'd put in the weekends and some of my savings. If I'm going to be out of work at sixty-two, I'd rather be out of work on land I helped build.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the extra three years give you compared to the fast one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to save and time to plan. It's like getting a warning about a drought in spring instead of in summer. You still lose, but you don't lose everything.

S3.say: I'd say five years is time to get ready the old way: work hard, save and look after your own. He'd add that the people pushing this don't live in towns like his.
S3.think: At sixty-three by 2031, he might make it near sixty-five if the mine keeps some older men on during the switchover. As the junior, he wouldn't count on it.
S3.do: Saves every spare dollar to double his cushion and tries to move to roof bolting or maintenance. Puts weekends and some savings into building up his son's beef block as a place to land.
S3.feel: Anxious, but with something to do about it.
S3.quote: It's like getting a warning about a drought in spring instead of in summer. You still lose, but you don't lose everything.
S3.fieldNote: Sam thinks about time in farming terms, which makes his answers vivid. His plan centres on family land rather than training or government help. The extra years shift him from alarm to anxious action.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long way off and a lot of these predictions don't come true. I'd say I'll believe it when I see a robot fix a broken belt nine hundred metres down. I'd keep my opinions for church and the kitchen table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I'd be sixty-eight and retired by then, God willing. So it's my grandkids I'd think about. I wouldn't change much myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working the shuttle car and get my roof bolter ticket. I'd keep saving and help my son on his block. I'd tell my grandson, who's sixteen, to get an apprenticeship in something you can't do from a computer, like welding or electrics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit doubtful about the whole thing, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why welding or electrics for your grandson?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because somebody has to build and fix the things, even the robots. And an apprenticeship teaches you to work with men who know more than you, which is a lesson I've learned again at fifty-eight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You doubt the predictions. What if it does come true?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'll be on the porch watching it, and I'll have done my part. The young ones will have to work it out, the way my father's generation worked out tractors.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a long way off and lots of predictions don't come true; he'll believe it when a robot fixes a broken belt nine hundred metres down. He'd keep his views for church and home.
S4.think: He expects to be retired at sixty-eight, God willing, so his thoughts go to his grandchildren. He wouldn't change much himself.
S4.do: Keeps driving the shuttle car, gets his roof bolter ticket, keeps saving and helps his son's block. Urges his sixteen-year-old grandson to take an apprenticeship in welding or electrics.
S4.feel: Calm and a bit doubtful about the whole thing.
S4.quote: I'll believe it when I see a robot fix a broken belt nine hundred metres down.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Sam is calm and sceptical, partly because retirement puts him out of reach. He favours apprenticeships for his grandson, true to his traditional outlook. He compares the change to his father's generation adapting to tractors.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, two years. I'd lose a second livelihood before sixty. What would help is the company keeping older men on in the jobs where hands are still needed, and being allowed to draw my pension early without losing half of it. I'd rather earn it than be handed it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. It's what got me through losing the farm. Whatever the machines do, I'll still be in the pew on Sunday, and that's something no company can automate.

headlineQuote: Whatever the machines do, I'll still be in the pew on Sunday, and that's something no company can automate.
portrait: Sam Petrov is a fifty-eight-year-old former dairy farmer who drives a shuttle car underground at a potash mine after the family farm was sold. He's a churchgoer who values hard work, family and self-reliance, distrusts both unions and government handouts, and has no interest in learning computers. He's calm if AI fizzles and uneasy with steady change, but AGI in two years alarms him because it would mean losing a second livelihood before sixty. With five years he saves and invests in his son's beef block, and with ten he's calm, sceptical and focused on his grandson's apprenticeship.
biggestWorry: AGI in two years worries him most, because he'd lose a second livelihood before sixty.
whatWouldHelp: The company keeping older workers on in hands-on jobs, and being able to draw his pension early without losing half of it.
